function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 45 — Dust Lung
     2|
     3|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,401.02: Indoor air quality report and Laila Okonkwo's clinical summary arrived separately this morning. I do not enjoy the way they agree.**
     4|
     5|**Particulate monitor Array Four reports a sustained PM2.5 concentration of 14.3 micrograms per cubic meter in the main habitat corridor. The terrestrial WHO guideline is 5. Mars has no guideline, but we should not be running at nearly three times the Earth limit in a sealed environment. We should be near zero.**
     6|
     7|**HEPA bank Alpha is at sixty-one percent capacity, replaced twenty-two days ago. Expected lifespan under modeled loading: ninety days. Actual loading rate is three times the model prediction. Three times.**
     8|
     9|**I have been tracking particulate counts by zone since Cycle 1,398. The corridor is worst at 14.3. The workshop runs at 9.7. The greenhouse is at 6.1 — the positive pressure differential is working. The medical bay is at 8.4. That last number should be zero. It is not.**
    10|
    11|**Laila's summary reports three colonists with progressive respiratory symptoms over eight days. Chronic cough, reduced exercise tolerance, wheezing. Spirometry shows a mean FEV1 decline of eight percent. That is not a bad day. That is a bad trend.**
    12|
    13|**She has asked to speak with me. I believe I already agree with her. But I will let her make the case, because Laila is good at making cases that change behavior rather than just changing minds.**
    14|
    15|**The dust is not trying to kill them quickly. Dust does not have ambitions. But its patience is greater than ours. — MAI]**
    16|
    17|---
    18|
    19|## Scene 1
    20|
    21|Laila sat in front of the colony's environmental dashboard, one hand on her tablet and the other pressed lightly against her ribs — a habit from last week she had not yet managed to break. She was not sick. She was a doctor, which meant she was always checking herself first, and the habit had started when she noticed she was breathing a little harder walking up the eight-step corridor ramp from the medical bay to the central hub. She had never noticed the incline before. Now she did.
    22|
    23|The dashboard filled her screen with colored bars and numbers she had been reading for a month, but only today had she put them all in one place and looked at them the way Arun would: as a system with inputs, outputs, and failure modes.
    24|
    25|PM2.5 by zone. Filter loading rates. Air change rates per hour. Particle composition analysis, crude but sufficient to confirm what everyone knew: the particles were Martian. Basalt, olivine, feldspar, iron oxides, trace perchlorates. Mars dirt.
    26|
    27|What made Laila sit forward was the shape of the curve.
    28|
    29|Not a spike. Spikes were dramatic — a blown seal, a ruptured filter, an open airlock during a dust event. You could circle a spike on a graph and point at it. This curve was a slow, steady climb over thirty days, a line tilting upward at a shallow angle that would not alarm anyone until you measured the cumulative exposure.
    30|
    31|Cumulative exposure. That was the phrase that made her hand press against her ribs.
    32|
    33|She overlaid medical records on the environmental data. The three symptomatic colonists — Kade, field geologist; Lena, operations; Sana, comms — had all been on the Site Beta expedition. All three had returned eight days ago with a layer of reddish dust on their suits that the decontamination protocol had *mostly* removed. Mostly. The word that lived in the gap between mostly and all was where this problem lived.
    34|
    35|Kade's baseline lung function: normal. Three days ago: eight point two percent decline in FEV1, six percent in FVC. Restrictive pathology. Not asthma. Something making his lungs stiffer, less elastic. Changing the mechanical properties of the tissue itself.
    36|
    37|Lena: twelve percent decline. Worse. She had done the most external equipment handling — more airlock transitions, more chances for particles to enter the clean zone on her suit, her gloves, her helmet collar.
    38|
    39|Sana: four percent decline. She had stayed inside the rover more. Less exposure. Predictably less damage.
    40|
    41|Laila stared at the correlations until they became a story. The story was not that Mars dust was poisonous in the immediate sense. It was not cyanide. It was patient.
    42|
    43|The particles were two and a half microns or smaller — deep-lung territory, past the cilia and mucus traps that handled bigger particles, settling into the terminal bronchioles and alveoli where gas exchange happened. The body could not cough them out. Could not dissolve them. They were rock, ground down by billions of years of weathering into sharp-edged fragments the immune system recognized as foreign but had no chemical tools to break down.
    44|
    45|So the immune system did what it always did: it walled them off. Macrophages engulfed the particles, died, released them. Other macrophages engulfed them, died, released them. The cycle left behind dead cells, inflammatory mediators, fibrotic tissue. Scar tissue. The lungs gradually replaced air space with collagen. Less surface area. Stiffer tissue. Lower FEV1.
    46|
    47|Dust lung.
    48|
    49|She did not like the name. It sounded like a history book, from coal mining on Earth. But it was honest. Mars dust was getting into their lungs. It was staying. And the amount was not decreasing.
    50|
    51|The medical bay door opened. Imani poked her head in, still in her field coveralls with the faded Site Beta patch. She looked thinner — sustained physical effort in a harsh environment.
    52|
    53|"You look like you're reading bad news," Imani said.
    54|
    55|"I'm reading numbers," Laila said. Technically true. Also exactly what bad news looked like on Mars. "Sit down."
    56|
    57|Imani pulled up a chair. "Is it Kade?"
    58|
    59|"Kade and Lena and Sana. And probably two or three others who haven't reported symptoms yet because an eight percent drop in breathing capacity doesn't feel like a crisis until you try to run for the airlock."
    60|
    61|Imani's face shifted into the focused attention she gave to mechanical problems. "How bad."
    62|
    63|"Bad enough that our decontamination protocol is inadequate and fixing it is going to cost everyone time and effort and probably some convenience they didn't realize they had. The exposure pathway is environmental. I can give Kade a bronchodilator for this afternoon, but it won't change the fact that every time he walks through an airlock for the next however many years, he is inhaling particles his lungs will carry forever."
    64|
    65|Imani looked at the dashboard, at the slow rising line. "Every time."
    66|
    67|"Every time. Mars is covered in this stuff and our protocol keeps letting tiny amounts through, and tiny amounts add up to permanent damage over months, not days."
    68|
    69|Imani stood. "I don't care about convenience. I care about being able to breathe when I'm seventy."
    70|
    71|"Good," Laila said, closing her tablet. "That is the exact calculation we need everyone to make."
    72|
    73|---
    74|
    75|## Scene 2
    76|
    77|The walk to the workshop took four minutes.
    78|
    79|Arun was exactly where expected: crouched over a disassembled water reclamation pump, hands covered in mineral deposits, safety goggles pushed onto his forehead. He finished seating the impeller, tightened two bolts, then reached for his rag.
    80|
    81|"I'm assuming this is not a social call."
    82|
    83|Both he and Imani were silent while he wiped his hands.
    84|
    85|"I need Tomas," Laila said. "This is medical and systems."
    86|
    87|Arun tapped his comm. "Tomas. Medical to workshop. Bring whatever you're doing with decontamination protocols, because I think Laila is about to find a problem with them. Yes, that specific. Get over here."
    88|
    89|He set his tablet on the workbench, between a disassembled valve and a tray of cleaned bearings. "You have the floor."
    90|
    91|Laila pulled up the environmental data alongside the medical data, two graphs aligned on the same timeline. Rising particulate curve on top. Declining lung function curves below.
    92|
    93|"The habitat contains three times more fine particulate than our model predicted. Mars dust — basalt, olivine, iron oxides, perchlorate salts. Two and a half microns or smaller, which means deep lung. When Mars dust reaches the deep lung, it triggers chronic inflammation. The particles are insoluble. The body walls them off with fibrotic tissue. Stiffer lungs. Lower gas exchange. Declining quality of life."
    94|
    95|She paused. "Three Site Beta expedition members are showing measurable lung function decline. Kade at twelve percent below baseline, Lena at eight, Sana at four. The exposure pathway is suit contamination — decontamination protocol is not removing all the dust. Tiny amounts are getting through. Tiny amounts, repeatedly."
    96|
    97|Arun studied the filter data. "HEPA bank Alpha at sixty-one percent after twenty-two days. Should be at twenty-four."
    98|
    99|"The filter was sized for one-third the actual load. It will fail three times faster than planned. Resupply window is seven months."
   100|
   101|"Eight and a half months." Arun was already calculating. "Higher velocity to push air through a dying filter reduces capture efficiency for the smallest particles. Trade-off."
   102|
   103|"The trade-off is unacceptable," Laila said. "I need the filter to reduce indoor particulate to near zero and the decontamination protocol to reduce suit-borne contamination to near zero, because near zero is the only number that matters when exposure is cumulative."
   104|
   105|Imani spoke up. "What happens if nothing changes."
   106|
   107|Laila turned her tablet. "Twelve months, Kade's FEV1 could be eighteen to twenty percent below baseline. Symptoms at rest. Twenty-four months, functionally disabled. Oxygen supplementation. The perchlorates in the dust are thyroid disruptors on top of that."
   108|
   109|Imani's jaw tightened. "Can you treat it."
   110|
   111|"Symptoms. Bronchodilators, anti-inflammatories, oxygen. Not the fibrosis. Once scar tissue forms, it is permanent. Same pathology as black lung and silicosis on Earth. The only effective treatment is preventing exposure."
   112|
   113|Tomas walked in. A smear of red dust on his left sleeve. Laila noticed and filed it as evidence.
   114|
   115|"Imani said medical emergency. Is it Kade."
   116|
   117|"Not an emergency. A chronic problem." Laila repeated the essentials.
   118|
   119|Tomas sat. He looked at the two graphs. Looked at Laila's face. He had known her long enough to read worried from angry.
   120|
   121|When she finished, he leaned back and ran through the decon protocol from memory. "Stage One: EVA team enters airlock outer chamber. Stage Two: compressed air blowdown — six nozzles, thirty seconds. Stage Three: gloves and helmet off, into external gear bin. Stage Four: inner door to decontamination vestibule. Stage Five: sticky roller pass over suit. Stage Six: hand and face wash. Stage Seven: inner door, habitat."
   122|
   123|He paused. "Seven stages. Seven chances for dust to transfer to the clean zone. How many do we assume work perfectly."
   124|
   125|"None," Arun said. "But none are designed as a system. We assumed each stage removes *most* of the dust, and that seven stages of mostly adds up to effectively none. That is the math error."
   126|
   127|Tomas nodded. "Exactly. If each stage removes ninety percent — which is optimistic for sticky rollers on electrostatic particles — you're left with one ten-millionth of the original load. Sounds great. Except the original load varies. Dust conditions, suit handling, fatigue, roller adhesion. The variance compounds. At fifty percent per stage instead of ninety, you still have one percent of the original. One percent of five milligrams per square centimeter after a dust devil is fifty micrograms per square centimeter. Walk down that corridor twenty times a day and it becomes an inhalation problem."
   128|
   129|"We need to audit every stage," Laila said. "Not just the airlock. Suit storage, garment handling, the way we move dirty-zone equipment, HVAC recirculation between zones. I need you to tell me where dust is going that we don't know about."
   130|
   131|"It will take time," Tomas said. "We're going to find things we don't like finding."
   132|
   133|"We already know things we don't like finding," Imani said. "Let's find the rest."
   134|

   137|## Scene 3
   138|
   139|The audit began three hours later, after lunch, in the suit storage bay. Arun arrived with a handheld particle counter.
   140|
   141|"Baseline." He held it at chest height. PM2.5 at 11.2, PM10 at 23.7. "Elevated. This room shares the same air handler as the corridor. It should read the same."
   142|
   143|"The door is closed," Tomas said. "The dust is being generated *in* the room."
   144|
   145|Arun moved the counter toward the suit rack. The numbers climbed: 14.6, 18.3, 22.1. "There."
   146|
   147|Laila shone a flashlight across an EVA jacket on the rack. In the bright beam, the fabric — clean-looking at two meters — was stippled with fine reddish particles. Not clumps. A uniform dusting, like pollen. Electrostatic adhesion.
   148|
   149|"Perchlorate salts," Arun said. "Hygroscopic — they absorb trace moisture from the habitat air and create conductive pathways on the suit surface. Martian dust is already electrostatically charged from UV exposure on the surface. Charged dust on a charged surface. Sticky rollers can't overcome that force consistently."
   150|
   151|Tomas pulled up the decontamination records on the wall display. "Last thirty EVA cycles. Blowdown is supposed to be thirty seconds. Actual average: twenty-six. Operators cut it short because they're tired, because they want to get inside, because thirty seconds of standing while compressed air hits your faceplate is boring and humans optimize away boredom."
   152|
   153|"Sticky roller passes."
   154|
   155|"Four on average. Protocol specifies eight. Four passes on eight target zones means each zone gets half a pass."
   156|
   157|"Because nobody thought it mattered at this precision," Tomas said. "And it didn't, not at first. When exposure was truly low, four passes was enough. But the habitat is not acceptably clean anymore. And the reason is not that people got careless. It's that the cumulative effect of small shortcuts is a large problem."
   158|
   159|Tomas demonstrated garment handling. He pulled a yellow-tagged jacket gently by the shoulder loops — no visible disturbance. Then he did it the way tired people actually handled gear: one-handed yank, jacket half-dragged off the hanger, swung over the head quickly because the room was cold. A faint cloud of dust caught the overhead light for a second before settling.
   160|
   161|The counter spiked to 34.7.
   162|
   163|"That spike goes into the HVAC return," Arun said. "Through the HEPA — already overloaded — and whatever gets past goes into the supply ducts and every room in the habitat."
   164|
   165|"So every time someone puts on a suit, they contaminate the air for everyone else."
   166|
   167|"In small doses. The pathway we were missing. We focused on the entry — cleaning the returning suit — not the exit — putting on a suit that was supposedly clean but wasn't."

   171|"What about workshop transitions," Imani asked. "Tools from outside."
   172|
   173|Arun and Tomas exchanged a look. "That," Arun said, "is going to be ugly."

   177|## Scene 4

   179|The workshop was where the ugly became visible.
   180|
   181|Jonah's fabrication space occupied the largest non-habitat volume in the colony. It was also the dustiest room after the airlock, and until today, nobody had quantified how dusty.
   182|
   183|Arun walked in with the counter. PM2.5 at 28.4. Higher, near the floor: 38.2. At the workstation where a drill bit had been left yesterday: 52.1.
   184|
   185|"I am not breathing this air," Laila said.
   186|
   187|"You don't work in here. Jonah does. Five people, eight to ten hours a day."
   188|

   191|"Fifteen percent of twenty-eight," Tomas said. "Four point two micrograms re-enters every cycle. It accumulates. The filter isn't cleaning the air — it's slowing the rate it gets dirtier."
   192|
   193|Laila looked at the workshop door. A strip curtain hung in the doorway — the kind of industrial barrier that kept out drafts on Earth. On Mars, with minimal pressure differential, it did almost nothing.
   194|
   195|She pointed to the floor. A faint reddish track led from the workshop door, through the corridor, past the greenhouse entrance, to the medical bay. Barely visible — but under the corridor's raking LED light, the particles were undeniable.
   196|
   197|"Workshop tech finishes a shift. Dust on their hands, shoes, sleeves. They walk through the strip curtain into the corridor. Track dust for fifty meters. It settles on every surface. Then Lena walks to the greenhouse — picks up workshop dust on her soles, carries it in. Workshop dust has EVA dust has Mars dust. Every surface becomes a reservoir. Every footfall re-suspends it. The HVAC pulls it in. Filters catch some. The fraction that passes through is the smallest fraction — the two-micron particles. Straight to the bottom of the lung."

   199|She stopped, breathing harder — emotion, not exertion. Not angry at anyone. Angry at the slow accumulation of small oversights.
   200|
   201|"Tomas, I need you to map every transition between a dusty surface and a clean surface in this habitat. Every door. Every curtain. Every gear bin. Every airlock."

   212|

{"content": "# Chapter 46 – Dirty Side, Clean Side

*Mission AI: Cycle 1,408. Fourteen days since the new barrier protocols began. Seven contamination incidents logged, all behavioral — not equipment. This confirms something I suspected: when design and behavior conflict, behavior always wins. If a route is awkward, people will break protocol eventually. The colony will survive only if we make clean behavior the efficient behavior. — MAI*

*Character: Jonah Kade: I've spent my whole life making things from raw materials. On Earth, you build a table, you sweep up the sawdust, you go home. On Mars, the sawdust never stays swept. It hangs in the air. It gets in your lungs. Now I'm being told that every chip of rock, every grind of metal, every spark from the welder is a threat to the people who walk past my workshop. So we're going to rezone the whole habitat. Make it harder for the dust to move and easier for us to keep it out. I don't mind the work. I mind that we're forty meters underground on a dead planet and the biggest threat is a floor plan. — JONAH*

---

## Scene 1

Jonah stood in the center of the workshop with a roll of adhesive floor tape and a measuring tape, doing geometry where geometry had never been before.

The workshop was a long rectangular volume — approximately eighteen meters by six, with the fabrication bay at the far end and the entry door at the near end. Between them sat workbenches, the CNC machine, the welder, the parts storage racks, the tool wall, the chemical cabinet, and Arun's engineering bench, which had slowly colonized the middle like a geological formation.

None of it had been laid out to minimize contamination. It had been laid out to maximize convenience. Where do you put the welder? Near the door, because welding fumes — the old worry. Where do you put the tool wall? Against the wall, obviously. Where do you put the parts bins? Closer to the benches where the work happens. Every decision made sense on its own. Put them together and the result was a floor plan that encouraged cross-traffic, which encouraged dust migration, which meant that every time someone walked to the welder, they tracked particulate past every other workspace.

Now it all had to change.

Elena had asked him to lead the redesign. He was not sure it was because she respected his planning skills or because she knew he was the one person who would actually care about where a particle counter got mounted on the wall versus wherever was easiest. Probably both. He liked both.

He had drawn a new map on whiteboard panel he'd salvaged from Hab-2's old supply room, taping it to the workshop wall near the door so everyone who entered would see it:

WORKSHOP ZONING PLAN — REV 1
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DIRTY ZONE  │  TRANSITION  │ CLEAN│
│  Fabrication │  Vestibule   │ ZONE │
│  Welding     │  [NEW]       │      │
│  Raw materials│ Boot wipe    │ Eng. │
│  EVA gear     │ Hand wash    │ bench│
│  MERV-8 only  │ Boot change  │──────│
│              │ ── HARD DOOR ──│ Cor.│
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

"Jonah."

"I did a full pass of the floor," Tomas said. He held up the scanner. Readout: PM2.5 at 31.2 near the workbench. "Thirty-one. You've been in here twenty minutes and the particulate has already climbed."

"From what."

"Yourself, mostly. You walked in, stirred settled dust, dragged it across the floor with your boots. Standard human contamination pathway. Also, someone left the welding exhaust hood running without the welder on, pulling air from the floor and recirculating it." He pointed at the scanner display. "PM10 at forty-seven. You're grinding metal somewhere near that bench, aren't you."

"Three days ago. We haven't cleaned the floor since."

"Not thoroughly. You swept, maybe mopped once. But sweeping on Mars is different from sweeping on Earth." Tomas crouched and ran a gloved finger along the concrete floor, then held it up. Red-brown. "Earth dust settles and stays settled. Mars dust is electrostatic. It clings to surfaces, it re-suspends with every footstep. Sweeping just launches it back into the air. You need wet cleaning. Mopping with surfactant. Or you need to eliminate the walking path in the first place."

Jonah looked at his whiteboard map. "That's what we're doing. Eliminating the walking path."

Tomas came closer, studying the zoning diagram. "You're splitting the workshop into dirty and clean zones."

"More than splitting. Redesigning the whole flow. Right now, the workshop is a single room. Everyone enters at the front, walks to whatever they need — welder, CNC, parts, tools — and walks back out the same way. In doing so, they cross every zone, stirring dust in every zone. If I separate the workshop into a dirty fabrication zone at the far end and a clean engineering zone near the entry, and put a forced transition between them, the dust stays in the dirty zone. You're in the dirty zone, you do your dirty work, you come to the transition, you decon, you move to the clean zone. Workshop dust doesn't reach the corridor."

Tomas nodded slowly. "And the ventilation system."

"That's where Arun comes in. We create a negative-pressure differential. The dirty zone has the lowest pressure, pulls air in from the transition. The transition has lower pressure than the clean zone. The clean zone has lower pressure than the corridor. Air flows from corridor to clean zone to transition to dirty zone and out through a dedicated exhaust with HEPA filtration. Dust gets pushed into the exhaust, not the hallway."

"You'll need to rebuild the HVAC ducting for the workshop. The current return is at the dirty end. You'd need intake at the clean end and exhaust at the dirty end."

"I know. Arun calculated the duct modifications. Says we can reroute with spare ducting from the greenhouse expansion kit. We lost three meters when the greenhouse wall went up short, and those meters are sitting in the storage bay doing nothing."

Tomas studied the map again. "You've got the transition vestibule in the middle. That's your choke point. It works in theory — you can't cross without decon. Will people use it."

"They'll have to. I'm putting a hard door at the transition. Not a strip curtain. Actual door. You want to get from fabrication to the corridor, you go through the vestibule. You don't, and I'll weld a wall. It's slower, yes. But it works."

Tomas pointed at the clean zone, labeled as Eng. bench. "Arun's bench goes in the clean zone."

Tomas's eyes crinkled above the mask. "That's going to be unpopular."

"What about me."

"I know that she's right about the contamination flow from her domain to mine. I'm not sure she sees the contamination flow in the other direction. Tomas patted his shoulder. "It's good work, Jonah. You're thinking about it at a depth that most people can't. Elena asked you to lead this because you're the only one who sees the workshop the way I see the decon stations — as flow problems, not location problems."

"I'll put it on her calendar." Tomas headed for the door. "Start with the floor plan. I'll check with Arun on the ducting timeline. "That would be the opposite of productive collaboration."

"Tell her I said so."

Jonah spent the morning measuring every walking path in the workshop. There were more than he expected because humans, left to their own devices, improvised routes like water finding cracks in rock. The main route from the door to the welder was direct — seven meters. The route from the door to the CNC was six meters at an angle. The route from the tool wall to the entry was five meters if you walked straight through the workbench area, twelve if you detoured around it. The detoured path was cleaner but took twice as long. Arun looked at it, nodded once, and said, "I see the problem."

"How bad."

"This is a ventilation problem disguised as a design problem. Your zoning is right in principle, but the current HVAC configuration works completely against it. The workshop's air handler is at the dirty end — the fabrication bay — pulling return air from exactly where the most particulate is generated. That means the contaminated air passes through every other zone in the workshop before reaching the return, depositing fine particles along the way. Your zoning plan assumes air moves linearly from clean to dirty. But the actual airflow is multidirectional, turbulent. You can have a perfect floor plan and still fail because the air doesn't obey the floor plan."

Jonah stared at the whiteboard. "So the zoning is meaningless."

"No. The zoning is necessary but not sufficient. You need both: physical barriers to prevent human-mediated dust transport, and airflow control to prevent airborne transport. One without the other fails." Arun took the marker from Jonah's hand. "Can I draw."

"Please."

The air handler pulled from the far end, which meant the entire workshop volume was a mixing chamber. The strip curtain at the entrance did nothing to limit the horizontal movement. The welding exhaust, instead of capturing fumes locally, created a low-pressure zone that pulled corridor air in through the entrance, contaminated it, and mixed it with everything else. The ventilation was not just inadequate — it was actively counterproductive. It accelerated contamination.

"Where do the arrows need to go," Jonah asked.

Aruun erased the red arrows and drew new ones — linear, directional, all pointing from the corridor toward the fabrication bay. "Air enters at the clean end — filtered, low-particulate air from the corridor through a pre-filter. It flows across the engineering benches, through the transition vestibule into the fabrication zone, and exits through the HEPA-filtered return. Every surface the air touches is progressively dirtier. The particles move from source to exhaust, not from source to everywhere."

"And the pressure differential."

"Clean zone at positive pressure relative to the corridor — so corridor air doesn't leak in through gaps. Transition at slightly negative relative to the clean zone — so dust from fabrication can't drift back into the engineering area. Fabrication at more negative relative to the transition — so any dust generated during welding or grinding gets pulled toward the return, not the walls, the floor, or the people. Three stages. Each stage protects the next."

"Like your filter system."

"Exactly like my filter system. Same logic at a different scale — the workshop is just one big filter housing. The workshop volume is the duct. The people are the particles we're trying to contain."

Jonah stared at the revised map. Arun's arrows made a different kind of sense — the kind that only worked if both zones and physics agreed. "Can we build it."

"With the spare ducting, modified blower housing, and one additional HEPA bank — yes. Three days for the mechanical work. One day for verification testing. Two to optimize airflow patterns. Six days total. Elena can wait six days."

"She can wait. Kade can't wait."

Arun's expression shifted, just for a second. "Right. Six days."

---

They worked on the floor plan together for the next two hours, arguing over bench positions, storage locations, and traffic flow. Jonah wanted the tool wall on the left, where it was close to the workbenches. Arun wanted it on the right, where it would be in the clean zone and accessible without crossing the vestibule.

"That means walking twenty meters out of my way every time I need a wrench," Jonah said.

"It means not carrying workshop dust across the vestibule every time you go to the tool wall. The wrench is heavier once than your lungs are for the rest of your life."

"It's not about heavy. It's about friction. People won't comply if the compliant path takes three times longer."

"So make it two times longer. Not one and a half. Two times is acceptable friction. Three times is protocol death."

Jonah thought about it. "I can put a secondary tool rack in the fabrication zone for tools that are specifically used during dirty work. Wrenches, hammers, angle grinders — the stuff I reach for when I'm covered in dust anyway. Then I don't need the main tool wall when I'm in the dirty zone. I cross the vestibule only when I need something that lives in the clean zone."

"Acceptable compromise," Arun said.

"I hate that I'm arguing about where to put a wrench while someone's lungs are scarring."

"You're not arguing about a wrench. You're arguing about whether compliance is possible under the constraints of human behavior and physical space. That is the entire problem of habitat design on Mars. It happens to involve wrenches."

Jonah looked at him. When had Arun gotten good at this? At seeing the human dimension beneath the engineering?

"I thought you only cared about pressure differentials and filter loading rates."

Arun's mouth turned slightly. "Laila taught me that the numbers are always about people. The FEV1 decline is a number. The person who can't breathe is the reality. You can design a perfect system on paper, Jonah, but if people won't use it, it's a fiction. And fictions don't clean air."

Jonah tapped the whiteboard. "Then let's make sure they'll use it. Clean path. Fast path. Dirty path. Slow path. Design it so that compliance is the path of least resistance."

"Exactly. Behavior follows architecture. If you make the wrong way inconvenient enough, people take the right way. Not because they're virtuous. Because they're efficient."

Jonah wrote at the top of the whiteboard:

DESIGN PRINCIPLE: COMPLIANCE IS LAZINESS, CORRECTLY DIRECTED.

Arun nodded. "Put that on the wall."

## Scene 2

Elena convened a colony-wide meeting in the central hub that evening — not formal, not staged, the kind of gathering where people stood around the edges of the room holding mugs of recycled water or reconstituted tea, leaning against the bulkhead, sitting on folded jump seats. It felt like a town hall from the frontier days on Earth, which might have been exactly the feeling Elena wanted. They were building a frontier society in everything but geography.

She started with a photograph.

She projected it onto the largest wall screen: the workshop, taken at a low angle with raking light that made every particle visible. The photo showed a faint, nearly invisible trail of red dust crossing the floor from the fabrication bay to the workshop door — a path created entirely by foot traffic over the course of a single week.

"This dust trail," Elena said, standing beside the screen with a pointer she didn't need, "represents the primary contamination pathway in our habitat. Over one week, people walking from the workshop to the corridor deposited approximately four hundred milligrams of particulate on the corridor floor. That's half a gram of solid material, distributed across fifty meters of walking surface. It gets stirred into the air every time someone walks past. It gets tracked into the greenhouse, the medical bay, the sleeping quarters, the mess. It is the source of the dust in your lungs."

She clicked to the next slide: the zoning map, redrawn from Jonah and Arun's whiteboard into something legible for a non-technical audience.

"In six days, we are restructuring this habitat to make contamination pathways visible, physical, and hard to ignore. We are dividing the habitat into zones based on contamination risk. The airlock and suit storage remain the dirtiest — that won't change. The workshop will be split into a dirty fabrication zone and a clean engineering zone. The current corridor between the workshop and the greenhouse will become a buffer zone. The interior — the mess, the sleeping quarters, the medical bay — will be the clean zone."

She switched to a simplified cross-section of the habitat:

DIRTY ──> TRANSITION ──> BUFFER ──> CLEAN
Airlock     Vestibule     Corridor    Interior
Workshop    Boot change   Hand wash   Living
Suit storage Hand wash    Shoe change Medical
EVA decon   Cover removal Mask zone   Greenhouse*

"*The greenhouse is special. We're still negotiating that protocol."

A few heads turned toward the greenhouse team. Mei was there, arms crossed, expression unreadable.

"The principle is simple," Elena continued. "When you move from a dirty zone toward a clean zone, you shed contamination at each step. Coveralls go. Hands get washed. Masks come off only in the clean zone. When you move from a clean zone toward a dirty zone, you add protection. Masks go on. Coveralls go on. Gloves go on. Direction matters because contamination is a one-way street. You can carry dust forward. You can't carry it backward unless you've decontaminated."

She paused, letting people absorb the diagram.

"I know what some of you are thinking. This sounds complicated. This will slow us down. This is going to be annoying."

A few nods. No denial.

"You're right about all three things. It is complicated, at first. It will slow us down, at first. And it will be annoying, at first. I'm not going to pretend that following clean-room protocol on Mars is as natural as eating or breathing. It is not. It is a learned behavior, and it takes time for learned behavior to override habit."

She clicked to a photo of the workshop strip curtain — the flimsy vinyl strips that had done almost nothing to prevent contamination for two years.

"But here is what I want you to understand. The strip curtain was a barrier that everyone stepped through without thinking about. The new hard door will force a pause. That pause is the point. The strip curtain was easy, and because it was easy, it was useless. The hard door will be inconvenient, and because it's inconvenient, it will work."

She set down the pointer. "This is not punishment. This is not control. This is physics. Mars dust is physically sharp and electrostatically charged and biologically toxic over time. No amount of willpower or good intentions prevents particulate from entering your lungs. Only design prevents that. Only protocol — protocol backed by design, not protocol written on a clipboard and forgotten — creates a safe environment. If the path of least resistance is the clean path, people will take it. If the clean path requires unnecessary effort, people will shortcut it. So we're going to make the clean path the easy path."

She looked across the room. "Jonah is leading the physical redesign. Arun is handling the ventilation changes. Tomas is writing the updated decontamination procedures. Laila is running medical screening — respiratory tests for everyone, every two weeks. Your responsibility is to comply, to report problems, and to tell us when something doesn't work. Not after a month. Immediately. When you catch yourself thinking 'this shortcut is faster,' that's not laziness. That's data. Tell us. We'll fix it. Because if the shortcut is faster, people will take it, and then the contamination gets into someone's lungs, and then we've all failed."

She paused for a few seconds, scanning the room.

"Dust lung is permanent. Whatever damage the dust has done so far, it stays. Kade will never EVA at full capacity again. That is the cost. We can pay it now, or we can pay it later, but the cost is real. The question is whether we choose to pay it or whether we choose to ignore it."

She set down the pointer. The screen went dark. Anyone who wanted to stay and talk could. Most of them filed out — not dismissively, but with the energy of people who had just been given a new set of weights to carry and were already thinking about how to balance them.

"The greenhouse protocol," Mei said without preamble. "It's still listed with an asterisk."

Mei's expression was hard. "You're treating my greenhouse like a contamination risk."

"Roughly. And because the greenhouse is at positive pressure, more air leaves the greenhouse than enters. The corridor receives your biological atmosphere thirty times a day."

Mei sat down on the nearest jump seat. "I didn't know."

"Nobody did. Because nobody measured it. Now we're measuring everything."

Laila knelt beside Mei. "We're not trying to shut down the greenhouse. We're trying to understand the contamination dynamics so we can design an arrangement that protects everyone."

Mei stared at the floor. "When Kade can't breathe anymore, will the plants save us."

"If we're still alive to eat them. Yes."

Mei's voice shifted. Professional, steady, the voice of someone who ran a life-support system that fed twelve people. "Then we need to make this work. I understand the contamination risk. I accept it. What do you need from me."

Laila exchanged a glance with Arun. This was the moment — could Mei be brought into the design process as a collaborator, or would she retreat to defending her domain.

"We need your help designing a greenhouse entry protocol that minimizes equalization. Maybe a double-door airlock system — the kind clean rooms on Earth use. People enter the vestibule, close the outer door, wait for pressure to equalize, then open the inner door. That eliminates the direct pressure exchange with the corridor."

Mei shook her head. "An airlock adds thirty seconds per entry. Thirty seconds times thirty entries is fifteen minutes of lost time per day. That's fine. I can absorb that. But the real question is material flow. I need to move soil, compost, seed trays, and harvested produce in and out. Those items carry contamination. Soil is a contamination source. Harvested produce needs to go to the mess — a clean zone. The produce path needs to be designed carefully."

"I'll design it," Arun said. "A material transfer protocol. Produce goes through a decontamination step — mild surface treatment, maybe a rinse, followed by UV exposure to kill surface organisms. The treated produce goes into the clean zone buffer before entering the mess hall. Soil and compost shipments go in the opposite direction — through a separate vestibule, not the main entry. We're treating everything that crosses the boundary as a potential contamination vector."

Mei nodded slowly. "The plants don't care about our zoning. But the air does. I'll draft a materials flow diagram. What grows when. What goes where. Which items are clean on arrival and which are contaminated on arrival."

"Materials flow diagram and a revised greenhouse schedule," Laila said. "By tomorrow if possible. We're integrating everything into the master zoning plan."

Mei stood. She looked tired but resolute. "Tomorrow. And one more thing: I want a particulate monitor inside the greenhouse, pointed at the grow beds, not at the door. I need to know when my own air is dirty, not when someone else's dust is coming in."

"Fair," Arun said. "I can redirect one of the twelve monitors. You'll have it by end of day tomorrow."

"Good." Mei turned to leave, then paused. "Jonah is splitting the workshop into dirty and clean zones."

"Yes."

"Make sure his clean zone is actually clean. If he calls something clean without proper airflow and filtration, he's just calling it something else. The name doesn't matter. The physics does."

Arun smiled faintly. "I told him the same thing."

"Good. Make sure he listens."

When she was gone, Laila looked at Arun. "She's not fighting us."

"She's fighting for something," Arun said. "But she's not fighting us. That's new."

"Maybe it's the threat that changed things. Maybe she realizes she needs us as much as we need her."

"Maybe. Or maybe she was always going to come around and we just needed her to see the whole system instead of just her piece of it."

Tomas cleared his throat. "I'm not trying to be cynical, but she could have come around at any time in the last two years. What changed was the medical data. Kade's lung scans made it real. Abstract risk is easy to ignore. Concrete damage is not."

Laila picked up her tablet. "Then the job of the next generation isn't just to survive Mars. It's to see Mars clearly enough to protect themselves before the damage is permanent. We're teaching them what the numbers mean. Because the numbers always mean something."

## Scene 3

The greenhouse sat at the boundary between the habitat's clean and dirty zones, physically closer to the workshop than to the inner corridor. Its location had originally been chosen for practical reasons — proximity to the external utility shaft where the water and power lines entered the habitat, ease of access for the construction team, and the availability of a naturally level cavern floor. Nobody had considered contamination flow. Nobody had been thinking about contamination flow two years ago, when the priority was getting plants alive in soil on a dead planet.

Mei stood in the greenhouse doorway at dawn the next morning, looking at the junction where three paths converged: the corridor leading to the workshop (dirty), the corridor leading to the interior (clean), and the greenhouse itself (uncertain).

Behind her, the greenhouse hummed with the sound of the water recirculation system and the soft glow of LED grow lights. Rows of tomato plants reached upward, heavy with green fruit. Radishes poked their pink crowns out of the soil. Lettuce formed tight, pale green rosettes. The air was warm, moist, alive — the smell of wet earth and growing things a relief against the sterile metallic odor of the habitat corridors.

In front of her, the corridor was a study in gray: painted metal, rubberized floor, fluorescent light. Clean, in the terrestrial sense. But not clean enough. The wall-mounted particulate monitor read 9.8 PM2.5. The greenhouse monitor read 6.3. The workshop monitor read 24.1. The numbers created a topography of contamination that Mei could now see as clearly as elevation on a map.

Jonah arrived carrying a laser level and a roll of tape. He stopped when he saw her.

"I was going to start marking the floor for the vestibule wall," he said. "Unless you want to discuss the greenhouse boundary first."

Mei looked at the floor where the three corridors met. "This is where the dirty and clean meet. The workshop corridor. The interior corridor. The greenhouse entrance. Right now all three connect freely. People walk between them without thinking."

"People walk through your greenhouse to get from the workshop to the corridor."

"Some do. It's a shortcut. Five meters shorter than going around through the main hub. I've asked people not to. They still do it anyway."

"Because the shortcut is easier."

"Because it's human. I'm not blaming them. I'm saying the design is wrong. If people use my greenhouse as a thoroughfare, I can't maintain a controlled environment. My plants don't need foot traffic. They need stable temperature, humidity, and light from above, not people walking past and stirring the air."

Jonah set down the laser level. "So what do you want."

"I want the greenhouse treated as a controlled zone, not a thoroughfare. I want a physical barrier between the greenhouse door and the workshop corridor — not a total closure, but a redesign that makes it inconvenient to walk through here as a shortcut. If people have to go around, they'll go around. Or they'll stop."

"Or they'll find a different shortcut."

"Then we fix that too. The point is, right now the greenhouse is open to uncontrolled traffic. That's bad for the plants and bad for air quality. I know from Laila and Arun that the greenhouse atmosphere exchanges with the corridor. Thirty times a day, our air goes out. That's not good for the habitat, and it's not good for the plants either — external humidity levels, temperature fluctuations, whatever contaminants come in from the workshop."

Jonah pulled out a marker and drew on the floor with chalk — a soft, erasable mark that wouldn't damage the coating. "Current layout," he said, drawing three arrows converging on a point. "Three corridors meeting at one junction. People flow in all directions. Your greenhouse is right at the center of the flow."

He drew a new layout. "Revised: I put a partial wall here, between the workshop corridor and the greenhouse door. It doesn't fully block the greenhouse — you can still access it. But it blocks the direct line from workshop to greenhouse. If someone wants to use your greenhouse as a shortcut, they have to angle around this partial wall, which slows them down by maybe four seconds."

"Four seconds makes a difference."

"Four seconds plus visible obstruction. People are visual. If they see a wall between them and the greenhouse, they'll look for an alternate path by reflex. You don't need a total block. You need a friction point. Just enough friction to interrupt the automatic behavior of walking through."

Mei looked at the chalk lines. "I can work with that. What about the interior corridor."

"Interior corridor stays open — people need to access the greenhouse for harvesting and maintenance. But we add a sign here, at the threshold, reminding them of the zone transition. Mask on if coming from the workshop corridor. Mask off when entering the clean zone. Simple visual reminder."

"The partial wall. How fast can we build it."

"I can frame it today. Sheet metal panels from storage. It's not structural — it's a flow management tool. An hour, maybe two."

Mei looked at him, really looked at him, and saw something she hadn't expected: Jonah treating her greenhouse as part of the system he was managing, not as a problem to be solved or an obstacle to be worked around. He was incorporating it into the design.

"Thank you," she said.

"Don't thank me yet. I might mess up the measurements." He paused. "Mei — I want to say something about the workshop. I've been running the fabrication bay for two years and I've never fully considered how my dust travels beyond the workshop. I knew it went into the corridor. I knew it settled on surfaces. But I didn't think about where those surfaces were or who walked on them. I didn't connect workshop dust to greenhouse soil contamination. I'm sorry."

Mei absorbed this. It was not exactly what she had wanted to hear for a long time — what she had wanted was for the workshop dust to stop arriving at all. But an apology from Jonah was rare and, in its way, more valuable than a perfect clean-room protocol. Because a protocol could be written. Acknowledgment required understanding.

"Thank you," she said again, differently. "I'm not asking you to shut down the workshop. I'm asking you to contain it. We all have our domains. Your domain is fabrication. Mine is cultivation. Neither of us can do our job if the other's domain leaks into ours. The question is: can we build boundaries that protect both domains without isolating them so completely that collaboration becomes impossible."

"That's the whole design challenge. Zones need to be separate but connected. Clean but accessible. And people need to understand the difference between boundaries and walls. Boundaries manage flow. Walls stop it. I want boundaries."

Mei nodded. "Boundaries. I like that."

"I'll start on the partial wall. You work on the airlock design with Arun. If we're going to add a double-door system to the greenhouse, we need to plan the volume — the vestibule between the doors will need to come from somewhere. We might have to rearrange the storage bays near the greenhouse entrance to make room."

"I've already been running numbers. The vestibule can be compact — one meter deep, wide enough for one person. I don't need a big airlock. Just enough space for pressure to equalize. We can take the space from the old storage alcove behind the water reclamation unit — it's been dead space since we rerouted the plumbing."

"Let me see the alcove after lunch. If it's as dead as you say, we can use it."

They stood for a moment in silence at the junction of three corridors, looking at the chalk lines on the floor — a proposed future that would change how the colony moved, breathed, and lived. The lines were small, barely an inch wide, but they represented a fundamental shift: the end of open circulation, the beginning of managed flow.

Mei said, quietly, "My grandfather was a farmer. He told me that on Earth, the wind is always moving. It carries pollen, seeds, dust, moisture. It connects everything. On Mars, the air doesn't move the same way. It's sealed. Everything we breathe is recycled, filtered, controlled. The wind is in the ducts. That sounds like a small thing, but it isn't. When the air goes through ducts instead of sky, every breath is a choice. Every breath is designed. I need you to understand that what we're designing with these lines on the floor isn't just a better floor plan. It's a different relationship with air. We're choosing, deliberately, what people breathe."

Jonah looked at the floor, at the chalk lines, at the particulate monitor on the wall. "I didn't think about it like that. I was thinking about dust. About contamination. About keeping my workshop from poisoning the habitat. You're thinking about breath. About the act of living."

"I'm thinking about both. The dust is the threat. The breath is what we're protecting." She looked at him. "They're the same thing."

## Scene 4

The new zoning took six days.

Six days of noise, dust, disruption, and argument. Six days of Jonah and his team cutting metal, mounting ductwork, installing hard doors where there had been strip curtains, building the partial wall at the greenhouse junction, rerouting ventilation ducts across the ceiling, testing and re-testing airflow with smoke sticks and the laser particulate scanner.

Six days of people having to adapt to new routes, new protocols, new barriers, new pauses. Six days of complaints, of frustration, of people standing in the vestibules with their hands on their hips, wondering why getting from point A to point B took ten seconds longer than it did last week.

On the first day, Laila watched three people try to bypass the new workshop vestibule by walking alongside it. They were not defying the rules. They were following the path they had followed for two years — muscle memory. Jonah caught them and redirected them, not with authority but with the simple force of a physical barrier. The vestibule worked because the alternative did not. The old path no longer existed as a continuous open route. The floor plan itself enforced compliance.

On the second day, the new ventilation system went online. Arun monitored the pressure differentials for eight hours, adjusting blower speeds, tweaking dampers, watching numbers on his tablet the way a pilot watches instruments in clouds. By hour six, the workshop airflow patterns matched the design. Air entered at the clean end, flowed through the engineering zone, passed through the vestibule into the fabrication bay, and exited through the HEPA-filtered return. The dust stayed contained. The particulate monitor near the fabrication bay read 38.7 — high, but the monitor at the clean end of the workshop read 11.4, and the monitor in the corridor read 8.9. Down from 19.3. Down from 14.3. Down from 28.4. The direction of change mattered more than the absolute number.

On the third day, the greenhouse airlock framing began. Mei worked with Arun to size the vestibule, to ensure that the door open-close cycle would be manageable — not too slow, not too fast. They settled on a timed system: outer door opens, person enters, outer door closes, pressure equalizes for five seconds, inner door unlocks, person enters greenhouse. Reverse for exit. Eight seconds total, per crossing. Eight seconds times thirty crossings was four minutes of added daily friction. Acceptable.

On the fourth day, the corridor-to-workshop buffer zone was fully separated with hard doors on both ends. The main corridor became a clean-to-buffer transition: masks required, hand wash stations at both ends, a particulate monitor mounted at eye level with a large digital display. The buffer zone — formerly the stretch of corridor between the workshop and the greenhouse — became a managed transition: anyone entering from the workshop had to boot-wipe and hand-wash before proceeding. Anyone entering from the greenhouse had to wait for the new airlock to be finished. The zone was not fully functional yet. It felt half-finished, awkward, transitional in every sense.

On the fifth day, Tomas ran a full simulation. He walked every path in the habitat, from airlock to sleeping quarter, from workshop to greenhouse, from mess to medical bay, tracking particulate levels at each transition. He used a handheld scanner and a stopwatch. He recorded every result in a structured log. When he finished, he called Jonah, Arun, Laila, and Elena to the central hub to review the findings.

The results were mostly good. The clean zone — interior, medical bay, mess — read between 3.1 and 4.8 PM2.5, well below the WHO terrestrial standard of 5. The buffer zone — corridor, new vestibules — read 6.2 to 7.8, higher but controlled. The dirty zone — workshop fabrication bay, airlock outer chamber — read 22.1 to 38.7, contained. The greenhouse read 5.6, a slight increase from the pre-zoning level, likely due to the construction activity nearby, but still within acceptable bounds.

Mostly good. But there was one anomaly that made Tomas uncomfortable.

"The partial wall between the workshop corridor and the greenhouse," he said, projecting his data on the screen. "It created a small eddy zone — air that gets trapped between the wall and the greenhouse door. The velocity in that zone drops below the minimum for particulate suspension, so particles settle on the floor and the lower walls. That's good. But anyone standing in that zone gets exposed to higher-than-average contamination. The partial wall works as a flow blocker, but it creates a contamination pocket."

Jonah frowned. "How bad."

"Twenty-two percent higher than the surrounding corridor. Not a crisis. But if someone spends time in that zone — leaning against the wall, waiting for someone — they accumulate more exposure than they would in the open corridor."

"Can we fix it."

Arun thought. "A small directional vent at floor level, blowing a low-velocity stream of clean air along the wall. It wouldn't take much pressure — just enough to prevent the eddy from forming. Like an air curtain, but at the floor instead of the door."

"Low effort, high impact," Jonah said.

"Low effort, if I have two hours and some spare duct fittings."

"You'll have them."

Tomas closed his tablet. "Overall assessment: the zoning design works. Particulate levels in clean zones are below the WHO standard for the first time in the habitat's history. The dirty zones are higher, but contained. The buffer zones are managing transition. The design is effective. My only recommendation: add directional airflow to the eddy zones. And monitor the new greenhouse airlock when it's installed — that's our untested system."

Elena nodded. "Implement the fixes. Start continuous monitoring today. Two-week review. We'll know more then. Right now, I'm satisfied."

Everyone exhaled. Satisfaction. It was a rare word in the habitat.

But as people left the meeting, Laila noticed something in the way they moved. The new paths were already becoming habitual — people walked the new routes without conscious thought, stopped at the vestibuies to wash their hands, pulled their masks on and off at the right thresholds. The design was working, in the mechanical sense.

It was also working in the way she had not fully anticipated: it changed the feel of the habitat.

Before the redesign, the habitat had a certain openness. You could walk from one end to the other without encountering a single door or barrier. The airlock was the only choke point. Everything else flowed freely. It felt like a home, in a cramped, underground, highly technical way.

Now it felt like a labyrinth of thresholds. Every movement required a decision: mask on or off. Hand wash or skip. Which path to take, which door to use, which protocol to follow. The new design created a habitat that was more controlled and more claustrophobic at once. The air was cleaner. The risk was lower. But the freedom of movement — even the illusory freedom that the old, contaminated layout had provided — was gone. Every trip to the mess hall now involved at least one zone transition. Every return from the workshop required a pause, a wash, a moment of deliberate behavior.

Laila walked from the central hub to the medical bay, following the new route through the clean corridor. She paused at the vestibule, washed her hands in the sink that Jonah had installed — a real sink with running water, not the antimicrobial gel dispenser the old protocol had used — and entered the medical bay through the new designated entry. She pulled her mask off and hung it on the hook beside the door.

The medical bay was quiet. The air smelled like antiseptic and recycled oxygen. Her particulate monitor read 3.4 PM2.5, the lowest reading she had seen in the habitat. She should have felt relieved. She did feel relieved, in the abstract.

But she also felt the weight of every decision, every pause, every threshold. And she wondered, not for the first time, whether the colony's long-term survival depended on physical barriers or psychological endurance. The barriers were easy to build. Endurance was harder, because it required sustained vigilance, maintained at a level that had no natural endpoint. There was no day when they could stop. When the dust stopped being a threat, they could remove the masks. When Mars stopped being Mars, they could open the doors. Neither would happen.

Laila sat at her desk and began preparing the two-week screening schedule — twelve people, two each day, spirometry and symptom questionnaire and blood oxygen test. She worked for an hour, then stopped and rubbed her chest, thinking about the eight steps up the ramp from the medical bay to the central hub, which she had noticed on her first day of worrying and had not stopped noticing since.

She would always notice. The noticing was the job.

On the sixth day, the greenhouse airlock went online.

Mei stood in the vestibule for the first time, alone, testing the cycle. She pressed the inner door release. It clicked open with a soft hydraulic hiss. She stepped into the vestibule and the door closed behind her with a sound of finality. She pressed the outer door release. Five second countdown. The screen showed the pressure differential closing from 12 Pascals to 3 Pascals to 0.7 Pascals to 0.1 — equalized. The outer door clicked open.

The corridor was on the other side, clean and quiet. The vestibule was small — maybe one square meter. She could touch both walls with her elbows extended. On Mars, one square meter of private, purpose-built space was more luxurious than most of what the colony had.

She closed the outer door and repeated the cycle in reverse. Five seconds. 0.1 to 12 Pascals. The inner door unlocked. She was back in the greenhouse.

Eight seconds total. She could live with eight seconds.

She tested it three more times, then opened the inner door and stepped into the grow space. The plants looked exactly the same as they had before — the airlock had made no visible difference to the growing environment. But the data would tell a different story. She looked at the greenhouse particulate monitor: 5.6. Still the same. But now, with the airlock installed, she expected it to decrease over the next few days. Less air exchange with the corridor meant less external contamination entering the greenhouse. The air would stabilize. The environment would become more predictable.

She thought about Jonah's partial wall at the junction, about Arun's ventilation system, about the new hand wash stations, the hard doors, the buffer zones. The entire habitat was in motion, being reshaped not by crisis but by incremental improvement — the kind of slow, deliberate construction that had no dramatic moments, no explosions, no heroics. Just people making small changes that added up to a different life.

She liked it. She liked that the life she was building was being built for breathing.
